forces: Voice (alto), alto flute, viola, guitar, vibraphone, xylorimba and percussion
performers: Marie-Thérèse Cahn, voice; J. Tiberge, flute; Collot, viola; A. Stingl, guitar; J. Delecluse, vibraphone; P. Naudin, xylorimba; A. Cavaille, percussion; Pierre Boulez, conductor
intro: Pierre Boulez conducted this recording of the complete Le Marteau sans maître for Vega, with Marie-Thérèse Cahn as the voice. The two sides of the LP are published as two parts, and this one holds movements I to V.

sections.label: C · III, “L’Artisanat furieux”, voice and flute

cues.title: Movement I: two duos
cues.text: Avant “L’Artisanat furieux” begins as two duos, flute with vibraphone and guitar with viola. After a short viola cadenza the four instruments mingle more freely.
cues.evidence: Jacques-Marie Lonchampt, programme note in the IRCAM work record: https://ressources.ircam.fr/fr/works/work/6981: “Avant L’Artisanat furieux débute comme un double duo entre flûte et vibraphone d’une part, et guitare et alto d’autre part”.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Domaine musical, 1956 season
cues.text: The sleeve calls this the fourth concert of the Domaine musical’s 1956 season, recorded under the auspices of the International Music Council with UNESCO’s help. Boulez had conducted the French première, with Marie-Thérèse Cahn, at the Petit Marigny on 21 March 1956.
cues.evidence: Recording credit: the Vega C 35 A 67 sleeve (note by Pierre Souvtchinsky, credits), scanned in the Internet Archive item https://archive.org/details/c-35-a-67-boulez-o-le-marteau-sans-maitre-pierre-boulez . French première of 21 March 1956 and Cahn: Philharmonie de Paris and French Ministry of Culture, Pierre Boulez archival biography, https://www.pierreboulez.org/default/biographie.aspx?_lg=en-US

cues.title: Movement II: flute, then xylorimba
cues.text: Commentaire I de “Bourreaux de solitude” is roughly in three parts. A long flute solo over the soft murmur of the other instruments is followed by a harsher section led by the xylorimba, then a brief return of the flute in a less relaxed mood.
cues.evidence: Jacques-Marie Lonchampt, programme note in the IRCAM work record: https://ressources.ircam.fr/fr/works/work/6981, on Commentaire I.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Central African wood percussion
cues.text: Boulez told Jed Distler in 2000 that the start of this second piece was “very much under the influence of central African music”, with its wood percussion and xylophone. In 1945–46 Mady Sauvageot, curator of music collections at the Musée Guimet, had introduced him to recordings from Africa and Asia.
cues.evidence: Boulez to Jed Distler, London, August 2000, republished 6 January 2016: https://jdistlerblog.wordpress.com/2016/01/06/an-interview-with-pierre-boulez-1925-2016/ . Recordings of music from Africa, India, Indonesia and Asia discovered through Mady Sauvageot, winter 1945–46: Philharmonie de Paris and French Ministry of Culture, Pierre Boulez archival biography, https://www.pierreboulez.org/default/biographie.aspx?_lg=en-US

cues.title: Nine parts, unequal silences
cues.text: Pierre Souvtchinsky’s sleeve note says the work divides into nine parts separated by silences of unequal length, each with its own meaning. The next movement follows one of those pauses.
cues.evidence: Souvtchinsky: “L’œuvre se divise en 9 parties séparées par des silences de durées inégales”; our translation. the Vega C 35 A 67 sleeve (note by Pierre Souvtchinsky, credits), scanned in the Internet Archive item https://archive.org/details/c-35-a-67-boulez-o-le-marteau-sans-maitre-pierre-boulez

cues.title: Movement III: voice and flute
cues.text: In “L’Artisanat furieux” the voice sings Char’s poem, which begins “La roulotte rouge au bord du clou”, with the flute alone. Lonchampt notes that this scoring cites “Der kranke Mond” from Schoenberg’s Pierrot lunaire, and that the melodic lines alternate between superposition and overlap.
cues.evidence: Jacques-Marie Lonchampt, programme note in the IRCAM work record: https://ressources.ircam.fr/fr/works/work/6981, on L’Artisanat furieux. Text of the poem, as printed on the Vega sleeve: the Vega C 35 A 67 sleeve (note by Pierre Souvtchinsky, credits), scanned in the Internet Archive item https://archive.org/details/c-35-a-67-boulez-o-le-marteau-sans-maitre-pierre-boulez
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Movement IV: no flute
cues.text: Commentaire II is the only movement without the flute. It moves in blocks of different lengths, separated by stops and sometimes filled with vibraphone resonance. The viola plays pizzicato until a section where it takes up the bow, and the triangle enters at the end of a rapid passage.
cues.evidence: Jacques-Marie Lonchampt, programme note in the IRCAM work record: https://ressources.ircam.fr/fr/works/work/6981, on Commentaire II.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Movement V: first “Bel édifice”
cues.text: “Bel édifice et les pressentiments”, first version, alternates unstable instrumental sections with entries for the voice over a more homophonic accompaniment. It is the first of two settings of the same Char poem; the second ends the work.
cues.evidence: Jacques-Marie Lonchampt, programme note in the IRCAM work record: https://ressources.ircam.fr/fr/works/work/6981, on Bel édifice et les pressentiments and on the three cycles (movements 5 and 9 are two successive versions of one text).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Baden-Baden, 1955
cues.text: Hans Rosbaud conducted the first performance on 18 June 1955 at the International Society for Contemporary Music festival in Baden-Baden, with Sybilla Plate as soloist. The work was chosen after a hard struggle within the French selection committee.
cues.evidence: Date, conductor and soloist: Philharmonie de Paris and French Ministry of Culture, Pierre Boulez archival biography, https://www.pierreboulez.org/default/biographie.aspx?_lg=en-US . Selection committee: Jacques-Marie Lonchampt, programme note in the IRCAM work record: https://ressources.ircam.fr/fr/works/work/6981

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Marie-Thérèse Cahn (voice (alto)), J. Tiberge (flute), Collot (viola), A. Stingl (guitar), J. Delecluse (vibraphone), P. Naudin (xylorimba), A. Cavaille (percussion), Pierre Boulez (conductor)
fields.note: Names as printed on the Vega sleeve, where each instrumentalist is preceded by “M.” (Monsieur) and not all have a first name. The Internet Archive description reads “Stingj” and “Cabaille”, which are misreadings of “Stingl” and “Cavaille” on the sleeve. The archival biography names Marie-Thérèse Cahn as the mezzo-soprano of the Domaine musical performance of 21 March 1956.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Nine-movement version as performed in the 1956 season, before Boulez’s revision of 1957; first of two files, holding movements I–V.
fields.note: The sleeve lists nine movements in the final order. The Wikipedia article and the archival biography place Boulez’s further revision, and the engraved Universal Edition score (UE 12450), in 1957, after this recording. MusicWeb’s review of the Accord reissue labels a 1956 recording by Cahn and Boulez, 30 min 44 s long, as the “1955 version”. The sleeve does not name an edition.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.value: 1956, season of the Domaine musical (fourth concert)
fields.note: The sleeve reads “Les Concerts du Domaine musical, 4me concert – saison 1956”, and Boulez’s 1963 discography reads “Enregistrement saison 1956”. Neither gives a day, and neither says whether the disc was made at a concert or in a studio session. The archival biography dates the French première, the first Domaine musical concert Boulez conducted in full, to 21 March 1956; the sources do not say that this is the fourth concert of the sleeve. A Discogs entry for the LP carries a contributor’s note “Recorded live in 1956” and names the Petit Théâtre Marigny as the place; the sleeve says neither, and the silences between the movements in this file contain only low-level noise.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No venue or studio is named on the sleeve. The Domaine musical gave its concerts at the Petit Marigny in 1956, but that does not establish where the disc was recorded.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Vega, 25 cm 33⅓ rpm LP, series “Présence de la musique contemporaine”
fields.note: The item description reads “C 35 A 67, disque microsillon 25 cm Véga”. The sleeve adds that the recording was made “sous les auspices du Conseil International de la Musique avec le concours de l’UNESCO”.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: L’Express of 12 November 1959 and Boulez’s 1963 discography both give C 35 A 67 as the “version intégrale”. The extracts disc, Vega C 30 A 66, is a different issue.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Side 1 (file f1): movements I–V; side 2 (file f2, labelled “fin”): movements VI–IX
fields.note: The item description lists f1 as “Le Marteau sans maître” and f2 as “Le Marteau sans maître (fin)” and does not list movements per side; Discogs lists A1–A5 as movements I–V and B1–B4 as VI–IX. In this file four silences of about 3.5 to 9 seconds end at 1:32, 5:25, 7:38 and 10:57, and the sound ends at about 14:07. They divide the side into five pieces of about 1:26, 3:50, 2:05, 3:12 and 3:10, which agree with the lengths of movements I–V in the 1956 recording as listed by MusicBrainz for a later reissue (1:30, 3:52, 2:06, 3:14, 3:10; 13 min 52 s in all). The side ends with the last movement of the first half, and the second side begins with “Bourreaux de solitude”. Matrix numbers are not shown.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The item is in the Internet Archive’s Hifidelity collection. Its description ends with a shelf mark (“Localisation: Af-10”), which suggests a library catalogue entry; no transfer engineer or institution is named. The uploader’s account is an email address, which is not reproduced.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item became public on 2 July 2021; that is an upload date, not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: The item offers FLAC, WAV and MP3 files for each side. Equalisation, noise reduction and speed correction are not described. The MP3 has about one second of digital silence at the start and about three at the end.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Boulez died in 2016, so the work is in copyright in the EU, under the life-plus-70 term, until the end of 2086.
fields.note: Boulez’s death on 5 January 2016 is recorded in the archival biography; the term is our calculation. The poems are by René Char, who died in 1988 and whose texts are also in copyright. Rights in the composition and in the poems are separate from rights in the recording. No United States status is claimed.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis: first published in 1956 (before 1963); US status not established.
fields.note: The archival biography lists the Véga record release of the work under 1956; L’Express lists the disc on 12 November 1959; Boulez’s 1963 book lists it. A French phonogram published in 1956 had run its 50-year term by the end of 2006 and was not revived by the 2011 extension, which applies to fixations still protected on 1 November 2013. No United States clearance is claimed. The Internet Archive item carries no licence and no litigation or restriction marker. The sleeve does not say whether the recording was made at a concert; a Discogs contributor’s note says it was recorded live. The basis here is publication of the commercial Vega LP, which L’Express documents by November 1959.

composer.epithet: Composer of music built on explosive attacks and long echoes, who also founded the ensembles, concert series and laboratories needed to perform it.
facts: Messiaen: harmony · Andrée Vaurabourg: counterpoint · René Leibowitz: twelve-note composition
Joined the Renaud–Barrault company in 1946, playing the ondes Martenot
BBC Symphony Orchestra, 1971–75 · New York Philharmonic, 1971–77
Domaine musical, 1954 · Ensemble intercontemporain, 1976 · IRCAM opened in 1977
composer.background:
Pierre Boulez arrived in Paris in 1943 after studying advanced mathematics in Lyon and turning down the engineering career his father wanted for him. He was eighteen and came from Montbrison in central France. Within two years he had won a first prize in harmony at the Conservatoire. His teacher, Olivier Messiaen, also held private classes in which students analysed Debussy’s Jeux and Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring.

Messiaen’s classroom required concentration. Horn and piano classes could be heard nearby while the students took musical dictation. ‘You learned to listen without sound’, Boulez recalled to Jed Distler in a London interview in August 2000, explaining why he never composed at the piano. He took counterpoint lessons with Andrée Vaurabourg and studied twelve-note music with René Leibowitz, who introduced him to the music of Schoenberg and Webern. By 1946 Boulez had broken with Leibowitz, impatient with his reverence for Schoenberg’s methods.
